suan-hua.appearance: Acid soil: seedlings stall, root tips go brown: start from what the field looks like, not from a bag. Wash the roots before you add fertilizer. If seedlings stall, the newest leaves open slowly and new roots are scarce. Do not judge from a yellow tint at the field edge. Pull one plant from the worst row, carry it to the ditch and rinse the mud. Do not rub the tips off. Then look: white growing tips, or brown stubby tips with few laterals. Brown, stubby tips look like aluminum toxicity from acid soil. Rust-colored irrigation water can support the diagnosis, but not every acid field shows it. Compare with the next ridge that is still green. Grain land and tea are not the same target. On grain land, consider agricultural lime only if topsoil pH is below about 5.5. Tea gardens should stay near pH 4.5–6.0; do not push them to neutral. This page helps you recognise the scene. Rates live in How to use lime, and with your local station.
suan-hua.conditions: Wet red-yellow soils, years of ammonium nitrogen, thin organic matter. Spring rain after rain pushes pH down.
suan-hua.plainExplain: When soil is too acid, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus will not hold, and aluminium dissolves onto the root tip. It is not a shortage of fertiliser. The root cannot take it up.
natural: Rain leaches calcium and magnesium. Red-yellow soils start low in bases.
Parent material holds aluminium that dissolves once the soil turns acid.
human: Ammonium nitrogen year after year, never a pH reading on this field.
Bald roots still chased with more fertiliser.
steps: Pull one plant from the worst ridge and rinse the roots at the ditch. Read the tips before you add fertiliser, because a bald tip cannot take a feed and urea will only burn what is left.

Test 0–20 cm pH. On grain land, consider lime only below about 5.5. Agricultural lime is commonly 50–150 kg/mu (about 750–2250 kg/ha), split in two; sandy soils take the low end. Not the same day as urea. No builder’s lime.
Do not push a tea garden to neutral. Tea stays around 4.5–6.0. Wait for new white roots, then a thin feed. Retest pH next season and stop once you are in range.
suan-hua.fieldCheck: Pull one plant and wash the roots. Brown, bald tips versus a green neighbour, then test 0–20 cm pH.
dontDo: Do not push tea to neutral as if it were grain land. Tea stays around 4.5–6.0.
Do not pour urea on bald roots. The feed cannot enter and will burn what is left.
Do not copy another field’s lime rate. Test this plough layer first.
suan-hua.whenToTest: Mix several points from the plough layer. A neighbour ridge is a useful pair. Retest pH the season after you amend.
prevention: Don’t let ammonium nitrogen be the only nitrogen source every year.
Rotted organic matter buffers the soil.
Retest pH the next season. Don’t stack lime year after year.
longform: pH is a measurement, not a disease. On grain land, consider lime only when pH is below about 5.5. The 6.0–7.5 band is where grain and vegetables are usually comfortable. Tea stays around 4.5–6.0; do not push tea to neutral.
One mu is one fifteenth of a hectare, so 50–150 kg/mu is about 750–2250 kg/ha. Split the dressing. Sandy soils take the low end. Not the same day as urea. No builder’s lime.
suan-hua.summary: When seedlings stall and the next ridge stays green, wash the roots first. Brown, bald tips mean test plough-layer pH. Lime only if it is below about 5.5.
suan-hua.commonCrops: Rice, peanut, maize, vegetables, citrus. Tea is acid-tolerant; that is a different guide.

suan-hua.mechanism:
In plain talk
Name what the field looks like before you talk bags. If roots or the soil surface do not match, fertiliser will not get in.
How it works
The plain point When the plough layer is too acid, aluminium comes off the minerals and burns the growing root tips. Once the tips are bald, water and nutrients stay out. The top looks like nitrogen or phosphorus shortage. More urea will not push through, and it can burn what roots are left. Aluminium hits the meristem first, so laterals fail. Calcium, magnesium and phosphorus also sit badly, but the first thing you can see is the root, not a missing bag of leaf feed. Liming is to let white tips grow again, not to paint the leaves. Washed roots brown and stubby; the next ridge still green; grain-land pH often below about 5.5. Southern red-yellow soils buffer poorly. Year after year of ammonium-N, and rain washing calcium and magnesium, push pH down. Tea likes acid. Grain does not want it more acid every year.
What you can see
Squat down: stall, scorch or crust should line up with the neighbouring row that still looks normal.
Name it before you fertilise
Do not push tea to neutral as if it were grain land. Tea stays around 4.5–6.0. Rates are ranges. Confirm them with the local station and the label. This page is not a lab.
suan-hua.example: The same grain field at pH 5.2 can discuss agricultural lime: sandy soil at about 50 kg/mu (about 750 kg/ha), split in two; clay can see the 150 kg/mu (about 2250 kg/ha) end of the range, still split. A tea garden at the same 5.2 often still sits in the 4.5–6.0 window. Do not copy the grain recipe onto tea. Not the same day as urea. No builder’s lime.

yan-jian.appearance: Saline soil: white crust and scorched margins: start from what the field looks like, not from a bag. Read the soil surface before you irrigate. Crouch: a thin white powder, or a crust you can peel. Emergence is patchy; leaf margins scorch and turn brittle. A light watering makes wilt worse — that is not drought. Pull one plant from the poor patch and one from the green ridge. Compare roots and margins. A white crust is a clue, not a prescription. Split salt from alkali. Salt is EC. Alkali is pH and exchangeable sodium. If the well is salty too, ask whether the drains work before you flood. Do not flood without drains. This page helps you recognise the scene. Leaching and gypsum rates live in the matching guides, with your local station.
yan-jian.conditions: Dry weather, salty groundwater, flood irrigation then a bake. Spring salt-rise is the clearest.
yan-jian.plainExplain: Salt makes the soil water harder for the root to drink, so a light watering can worsen wilt.
natural: Little rain, so salt cannot leach.
Salty groundwater lifts salt to the surface.
human: A white crust treated as a potassium gap.
Flooding a field with no drain lifts salt higher.
steps: Crouch and read the surface: powder, crust, a dripper ring. Photograph the poor patch next to the green neighbour. Split salt from alkali before the next bag.
The ditch must run. Thin the feed first. Frequent light watering lifts salt; only a working ditch can leach. If the well is salty, ask about the ditch first.
High pH and mud-then-board can discuss alkali amendment. Gypsum is not for every white crust. Rates live in the saline guides; confirm with a local station.
yan-jian.fieldCheck: Crouch and read the surface: a thin white powder, or a crust you can peel.
dontDo: Do not throw gypsum at every white crust.
Do not flood without a ditch.
Do not treat worse wilt after watering as more drought.
yan-jian.whenToTest: One bag from the thick crust, one from a clean emergence patch. In spring, read EC, pH and sodium.
prevention: Wash only with a drain. Cover cuts the rise.
Keep fertiliser mild. Stop high-salt bags on the patch.

yan-jian.mechanism:
In plain talk
Name what the field looks like before you talk bags. If roots or the soil surface do not match, fertiliser will not get in.
How it works
The plain point Salt makes the soil water harder to drink, so a light watering wilts plants more. High sodium also pulls crumbs apart: mud when wet, a board when dry. Little and often is an elevator for salt to the surface. Gypsum is for sodic alkali, not for every white crust. Dry irrigation districts, the coast and greenhouse emitters see this most. White powder or a peelable crust, patchy emergence, scorched margins, worse wilt after a sip of water. Mud-then-board points to sodium — do not treat it as salt alone with a flood.
What you can see
Squat down: stall, scorch or crust should line up with the neighbouring row that still looks normal.
Name it before you fertilise
Do not throw gypsum at every white crust. Rates are ranges. Confirm them with the local station and the label. This page is not a lab.

ban-jie.appearance: Hard soil: a shiny pan the roots will not cross: start from what the field looks like, not from a bag. Try the hoe and the roots before you feed. After rain, a slurry; when dry, a cap that bounces the blade. Seedlings wear a cap of soil; roots run sideways. Dig in the wheel track and the poor patch. Look about 20 cm down for a shiny, knife-cut pan. If a footprint sinks deep in wet soil, keep the tractor off. If the next ridge still takes the hoe, put the two profiles side by side. A pan blocks the road for roots. It is not simply a missing bag of fertiliser Confirm rates with the local station and the label.
ban-jie.conditions: Years of shallow rotavating, traffic on wet soil, thin organic matter. The day after rain shows it.
ban-jie.plainExplain: Repeated traffic, wet tillage and thin organic matter flatten aggregates and close pores.
natural: Clay shrinks when it dries; raindrops seal the surface.
A plough pan perches water so roots cannot pass.
human: Rotavating wet soil packs the path harder.
Shallow passes every year polish the pan.
steps: Keep machines off wet soil. Deep prints polish the pan and make the next loosening harder.
Dig a pit and look at about twenty centimetres for a shiny pan. Subsoil only when the soil cracks instead of smearing, and only through that layer.
Follow with rotted organic matter to keep pores. One wet, deep inversion will polish the face again.
ban-jie.fieldCheck: Try the hoe: after rain a slurry, when dry a cap that bounces the blade.
dontDo: Do not drive on wet soil.
Do not subsoil a slurry.
Do not chase compaction with more fertiliser.
ban-jie.whenToTest: Sample above and below the pan. Don’t mix them in one bag.
prevention: No traffic, no rotavator, on wet soil.
Deep-loosen on the right moisture, just through the pan.
Organic matter rebuilds crumbs. Iron alone will not.

ban-jie.mechanism:
In plain talk
Name what the field looks like before you talk bags. If roots or the soil surface do not match, fertiliser will not get in.
How it works
The plain point Repeated traffic, wet tillage and thin organic matter squash crumbs and close pores. Roots hit the pan and turn. Water and air do not pass. Driving on wet soil is the fastest way to a plough pan. Deep loosening only when the soil fractures, not smears. One layer near 20 cm is enough — do not invert a wet profile. Water sitting after rain, a bouncing hoe, roots running sideways, seedlings in a soil cap. Worst in the ruts.
What you can see
Squat down: stall, scorch or crust should line up with the neighbouring row that still looks normal.
Name it before you fertilise
Do not drive on wet soil. Rates are ranges. Confirm them with the local station and the label. This page is not a lab.

you-ji-zhi.appearance: Thin organic matter: pale soil that will not hold a ball: start from what the field looks like, not from a bag. Rub a handful before you name a bag. Plough-layer soil that is pale, powdery, will not hold a ball and runs through the fingers. Fertiliser after one rain looks as if you never applied it. Bare ground in winter and spring drops fastest. If the next ridge still makes a ball, put the two handfuls together. Pale colour is not a lab sheet, but pale soil is often thin in organic matter. Sand holds even less. Do not expect a packet of microbes to put the layer back in one season. Organic matter is a reserve, not a brand of inoculant Confirm rates with the local station and the label.

human: All straw leaves the field; fertiliser is asked to rebuild the house.
A microbe bag treated as a one-season rescue.

Return straw and add rotted manure for several years. Sandy soils, little and often. Do not bury raw manure against the root.
The organic-matter cell is a reserve, not a bag count. This season’s fertiliser lives on the matching nutrient or sandy-soil page, with a local station.

you-ji-zhi.mechanism:
In plain talk
Name what the field looks like before you talk bags. If roots or the soil surface do not match, fertiliser will not get in.
How it works
The plain point Organic matter is the soil’s meat. When it is thin, fertiliser will not stay, and aluminium and salt problems show sooner. Taking grain and leaving no straw, plus burying raw manure, thins the layer year after year. Inoculant is not the product name for organic matter. Three years of straw return plus composted manure beats one dump. On sand, little and often. Pale colour, a handful that falls apart, a field that dries through after rain. Yellow leaves are extra, not the first test.
What you can see
Squat down: stall, scorch or crust should line up with the neighbouring row that still looks normal.
Name it before you fertilise
Do not bury raw manure against the root. Rates are ranges. Confirm them with the local station and the label. This page is not a lab.

que-dan.appearance: Nitrogen: old leaves yellow, new leaves still green: start from what the field looks like, not from a bag. Read which leaves, then the roots. Old leaves evenly yellow, newest leaves still green, the plant still extending, washed roots white: that looks like nitrogen. If the newest leaves yellow too, think sulphur or iron. Black, smelly roots or standing water: do not call it nitrogen yet. Pick old leaves from the yellowest row and the green ridge, and wash a root from each. If leaf position does not match, do not rush urea. Urea is not the name of every yellow leaf Confirm rates with the local station and the label.
que-dan.conditions: Nitrogen moves. Old leaves feed the new ones. Sand will not hold a whole-year dump.
que-dan.plainExplain: Nitrogen moves from old leaves to new ones, so shortage yellows old leaves first.
natural: Nitrogen moves; old leaves yellow first.

human: New leaves yellow and still chased as nitrogen.

steps: Read leaf position and roots. Old leaves evenly yellow, new leaves green, roots white: then nitrogen is on the table. If position does not match, do not add urea.
Rule out waterlogging and spray injury. Standing water or black roots: drain first; nitrogen cannot enter.

Do not call every yellow leaf nitrogen.
Do not treat yellow new leaves with green veins as nitrogen.
que-dan.whenToTest: Note the lower yellow leaves and the green top, then sample the plough layer.
prevention: Split nitrogen only while roots are white.

lao-hai.appearance: Waterlogging: wilt by day, wet soil, black roots: start from what the field looks like, not from a bag. Look for standing water, then pull a root. Wilt on wet soil is not drought. In plain talk
Name what the field looks like before you talk bags. If roots or the soil surface do not match, fertiliser will not get in.
How it works
In strongly acid soil, aluminium injures the meristem of the tip. Once the mouth is gone, later fertiliser cannot enter. The fix is to lift plough-layer pH past the injury threshold — on grain land, consider lime only below about 5.5 — not more nitrogen. Thin organic matter buffers poorly. Tea tolerates acid; do not use the grain target on tea.
What you can see
Squat down: stall, scorch or crust should line up with the neighbouring row that still looks normal.
Name it before you fertilise

Don’t keep deep water and pour nitrogen; don’t double compound on black roots. Rates are ranges. Confirm them with the local station and the label. This page is not a lab.
